claim: More than 7% of deaths among children under 5 years in the world are attributable to malaria.
source: Malaria remains a major public health challenge, with more than 7% of deaths among children under 5 years in the world attributable to the disease (Liu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2012.

claim: 80% of malaria cases occur in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: In sub-Saharan Africa alone where 80% of malaria cases occur (World Health Organization, 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to World Health Organization, 2012.

claim: District coverage rates in sub-Saharan Africa are estimated at over 70% for the third dose of diphtheria–tetanus–pertussis (DTP) vaccines.
source: district coverage rates are estimated at over 70% for the third dose of diphtheria–tetanus–pertussis (DTP) vaccines and 75% for measles-containing vaccines (World Health Organization and UNICEF, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to World Health Organization and UNICEF, 2013.

claim: District coverage rates in sub-Saharan Africa are estimated at 75% for measles-containing vaccines.

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to World Health Organization and UNICEF, 2013.

claim: Injection with live strains of Bacille Calmette Guerin (BCG) vaccine may confer sterilizing protection against Plasmodium infection in murine models.
source: In particular, early evidence from murine models indicates that injection with live strains of Bacille Calmette Guerin (BCG) vaccine may confer sterilizing protection against Plasmodium infection (Clark et al., 1976).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Clark et al., 1976, describing evidence from murine models.

claim: The protective effect of BCG against Plasmodium infection in murine models depends on several factors including route of administration, type of immunogen used, vaccine schedule in relation to malaria exposure, mouse strain, sex, and Plasmodium species tested.
source: However, this effect seems to depend on several factors including route of administration (intradermal, subcutaneous, intramuscular vs intravenous), type of immunogen used (killed vs live attenuated), vaccine schedule in relation to malaria exposure (before vs after infection), mouse strain, sex, and Plasmodium species tested (Clark et al., 1976; Smrkovski and Strickland, 1978, Smrkovski, 1981, 1982; Murphy, 1981, Matsumoto et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies examining these factors.

claim: The risk of malaria infection has been thought to increase during downregulation in cellular immunity and T helper (Th) 2 cell upregulation following measles infection and/or immunization.
source: Conversely, the risk of malaria infection has been thought to increase during downregulation in cellular immunity (including interleukin-12, interferon-gamma, T cells) and T helper (Th) 2 cell upregulation following measles infection and/or immunization (Desai et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Desai et al., 2005.

claim: Epidemiological evidence to support the theory that measles infection/immunization increases malaria risk in humans remains unclear.
source: Epidemiological evidence to support this theory in humans remains unclear (Whittle et al., 1980; Rooth and Bjorkman, 1992).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Whittle et al., 1980 and Rooth and Bjorkman, 1992.

claim: Multiple clinical trials in infants and young children have identified protective effects from vitamin A supplementation against malaria illness.
source: Multiple clinical trials in infants and young children have also identified protective effects from vitamin A supplementation against illness (number and time to first clinical episode, risk of febrile illness, spleen enlargement, and mean parasite density) (Shankar et al., 1999; Zeba et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to clinical trials by Shankar et al., 1999 and Zeba et al., 2008.

claim: Multiple clinical trials in infants and young children have identified protective effects from vitamin A supplementation against death caused by malaria.
source: and death caused by malaria (Fawzi et al., 1999; Varandas et al., 2001; Mwanga-Amumpaire et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to clinical trials by Fawzi et al., 1999; Varandas et al., 2001; and Mwanga-Amumpaire et al., 2012.

claim: Vitamin A is thought to act as a regulator of pro-inflammatory response genes and phagocytotic clearance of Plasmodium falciparum-infected erythrocytes through its active metabolite, retinoic acid.
source: Vitamin A is thought to act as a regulator of pro-inflammatory response genes (e.g. tumor necrosis factor alpha) and phagocytotic clearance (e.g. cluster of differentiation 36 [CD36]) of Plasmodium falciparum-infected erythrocytes, by way of its active metabolite, retinoic acid (SanJoaquin and Molyneux, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to SanJoaquin and Molyneux, 2009.

claim: Vitamin A did not appear to modulate the risk of parasitemia in a clinical trial study of Ghanaian children.
source: While vitamin A did not appear to modulate the risk of parasitemia in a clinical trial study of Ghanaian children (Binka et al., 1995)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a clinical trial by Binka et al., 1995.

claim: Vitamin A did not appear to modulate the risk of parasitemia in Tanzanian children previously hospitalized with pneumonia.

claim: A cluster randomized intervention trial for breastfeeding in Uganda observed a sixfold decrease in the adjusted risk of malaria infection among children receiving vitamin A.

claim: An apparent increase in levels of parasitemia was observed in mouse models when combining vitamin A supplements with DTP vaccination, with an effect thought to be stronger among female mice.

claim: Chagas is not endemic to the countries studied (Burkina Faso, Mozambique, Rwanda, and Senegal).
source: Although Chagas is not endemic to the countries we studied (Morel and Lazdins, 2003)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Morel and Lazdins, 2003.

claim: There is growing evidence that schistosomiasis may be an overlooked, endemic disease among infants and young children in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: there is growing evidence that schistosomiasis may be an overlooked, endemic disease among infants and young children in sub-Saharan Africa (Russell Stothard et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Russell Stothard et al., 2013.

claim: The study represents an active population-based surveillance of malaria infection within four countries.
source: Our study represents an active population-based surveillance of malaria infection within four countries.
evidence: The claim describes the study design.

claim: The breadth and size of the study population enabled evaluation of the association between malaria and childhood vaccines/vitamin A despite high vaccination coverage rates.
source: The breadth and size of the study population enabled us to evaluate the association between malaria and childhood vaccines/vitamin A despite high vaccination coverage rates within most of the communities surveyed (Desai et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim describes a strength of the study design.

claim: When Mozambique data were excluded from blood film analysis, the magnitude of protective vitamin A effects in both blood film and antigenemia models were nearly identical.
source: This analysis showed that when Mozambique data were excluded from blood film analysis, the magnitude of protective vitamin A effects in both blood film and antigenemia models were nearly identical.
evidence: The claim is based on sensitivity analysis conducted by the authors.

claim: Blood films were likely to be detecting P. falciparum due to geography.
source: However, due to geography, blood films were likely to be detecting P. falciparum due to geography (Gething et al., 2011, 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on inference supported by citations regarding P. falciparum geography.

claim: Vitamin A is fat soluble and can be stored in the liver for long periods of time.
source: Given that vitamin A is fat soluble and can be stored in the liver for long periods of time (Blomhoff, 1994; Tanumihardjo, 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Blomhoff, 1994 and Tanumihardjo, 2011.

claim: There is a time lag between rainfall and vegetation response, as dormant vegetation does not immediately become green following the return of seasonal rains.
source: Foremost among these concerns is the time lag between rainfall and vegetation response, as dormant vegetation does not immediately become green following the return of seasonal rains (Nicholson et al., 1990; Davenport and Nicholson, 1993).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nicholson et al., 1990 and Davenport and Nicholson, 1993.

claim: There is a similarly lagged response to rainfall in populations of vector species responsible for spreading Plasmodium.
source: However, this concern will be partially mitigated by a similarly lagged response to rainfall in populations of vector species responsible for spreading Plasmodium (Mbogo et al., 2003; Galardo et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mbogo et al., 2003 and Galardo et al., 2009.

claim: Forests tend to retain more green vegetation (and thus have higher EVI values) even when dry due to deeper root systems.
source: This issue is most apparent when comparing dry season EVI values in grasslands to those in forests, as forests tend to retain more green vegetation (and thus have higher EVI values) even when dry due to deeper root systems, etc.
evidence: The claim is based on established ecological knowledge about vegetation responses.

claim: Plants in drier ecosystems have evolved to respond more quickly to infrequent rain events.
source: A second aspect of EVI linked to land cover differences is the speed at which vegetation responds to rainfall, as plants in drier ecosystems have evolved to respond more quickly to infrequent rain events (Ogle and Reynolds, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ogle and Reynolds, 2004.

claim: HIV is an established risk factor for malaria infection.
source: Finally, data on children's HIV status were not available. Although the possibility of mother-to-child HIV transmission was low in our study (less than 1% of mothers were HIV positive), HIV is an established risk factor for malaria infection (Abu-Raddad et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Abu-Raddad et al., 2006.

claim: The protective association between vitamin A and malaria remained after adjusting for maternal HIV status in a subgroup of models.
source: To address this issue, we adjusted a subgroup of models for maternal HIV status. While the protective association between vitamin A and malaria remained, the low prevalence of maternal HIV in our study population (and hence low statistical power) makes it difficult to rule out potential vitamin A–HIV interactions.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis adjusting for maternal HIV status.

claim: Data were extracted from Macro International Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS), a database of nationally representative household surveys conducted in low and middle-income countries.
source: Data were extracted from Macro International Demographic and Health Surveys (DHS) (ICF International, 2013), a database of nationally representative household surveys conducted in low and middle-income countries.
evidence: The claim describes the data source for the study.

claim: The study focused on standard DHS surveys carried out since January 2010, which tested children for malaria using blood films and documented children's use of standard vaccines and vitamin A supplements.
source: We focused on standard DHS surveys carried out since January 2010, which tested children for malaria using blood films (gold standard malaria test) and documented children's use of standard vaccines and vitamin A supplements.
evidence: The claim describes the study inclusion criteria.

claim: From 20 country surveys with accessible data, four surveys fitted the study criteria (Burkina Faso, Mozambique, Rwanda, and Senegal).
source: From 20 country surveys with accessible data (last checked 15 January 2014), we identified four surveys that fitted these criteria (i.e. Burkina Faso, Mozambique, Rwanda, and Senegal).
evidence: The claim describes the study selection process.

claim: All surveys were conducted between May 2010 and November 2011.
source: All surveys were conducted between May 2010 and November 2011, and used a multistage sampling process, by which study participants were identified from randomly selected households within a primary sampling unit (PSU) (e.g. census enumeration tract).
evidence: The claim describes the timing of data collection.

claim: The surveys used a multistage sampling process, by which study participants were identified from randomly selected households within a primary sampling unit (PSU).
source: All surveys were conducted between May 2010 and November 2011, and used a multistage sampling process, by which study participants were identified from randomly selected households within a primary sampling unit (PSU) (e.g. census enumeration tract).
evidence: The claim describes the sampling methodology.

claim: Trained interviewers used standardized questionnaires to collect information from participants during home interviews on a range of issues related to population, health, and nutrition.
source: Trained interviewers used standardized questionnaires to collect information from participants during home interviews on a range of issues related to population, health, and nutrition.
evidence: The claim describes the data collection methodology.

claim: Geographical waypoints (World Geodetic System 84 datum, latitude, and longitude) were recorded at the center of each PSU.
source: Geographical waypoints (World Geodetic System 84 datum, latitude, and longitude) were also recorded at the center of each PSU.
evidence: The claim describes the geographical data collection.

claim: Eligible subjects for the analysis included children 6–59 months of age who provided blood samples for malaria screening and had their history of vaccination and vitamin A supplementation documented based on health records.
source: Eligible subjects for our analysis included children 6–59 months of age who, during survey interviews, provided blood samples for malaria screening and had their history of vaccination and vitamin A supplementation documented based on health records.
evidence: The claim describes the study eligibility criteria.

claim: An EVI dataset was used to estimate seasonality as it relates to seasonal precipitation and the emergence of vector mosquito species.
source: To estimate seasonality, an EVI dataset was used as it relates to seasonal precipitation, albeit lagged in time, and the emergence of vector mosquito species.
evidence: The claim describes the methodology for estimating seasonality.

claim: The EVI dataset was created from moderate resolution imaging spectroradiometer (MODIS) bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF)-corrected composites (MCD43B4).
source: This dataset was created from moderate resolution imaging spectroradiometer (MODIS) bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF)-corrected composites (MCD43B4) (Schaaf et al., 2002), which have a 1 km spatial resolution and a 16-day temporal resolution.
evidence: The claim describes the data source for EVI with citation.

claim: The MODIS BRDF-corrected composites have a 1 km spatial resolution and a 16-day temporal resolution.
source: This dataset was created from moderate resolution imaging spectroradiometer (MODIS) bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF)-corrected composites (MCD43B4) (Schaaf et al., 2002), which have a 1 km spatial resolution and a 16-day temporal resolution.
evidence: The claim describes the technical specifications of the MODIS data.

claim: By utilizing MODIS data from sensors located on both the Aqua and Terra satellite platforms, the temporal resolution of the final EVI dataset was increased to 8 days, or 46 grids per year.
source: By utilizing MODIS data from sensors located on both the Aqua and Terra satellite platforms, the temporal resolution of the final EVI dataset was increased to 8 days, or 46 grids (i.e. rasters or images) per year.
evidence: The claim describes the methodology for improving temporal resolution.

claim: EVI was calculated for each mosaic using the equation defined by Huete et al. (1999).
source: EVI was then calculated for each mosaic using the equation defined by Huete et al. (1999).
evidence: The claim describes the calculation method with citation.

claim: A cloud-filling algorithm was applied to each EVI grid to create a spatially complete dataset.
source: Due to cloud cover, which was particularly problematic in forested regions of equatorial west Africa, a cloud-filling algorithm was applied to each EVI grid to create a spatially complete dataset (Weiss et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim describes the data processing methodology with citation.

claim: Predicted allele frequencies for HbS were extracted for each PSU waypoint from continuous global predicted surface maps.
source: Predicted allele frequencies for HbS (Piel et al., 2013) and G6PDd (Howes et al., 2012) were extracted for each PSU waypoint from continuous global predicted surface maps of the worldwide distribution of these genes using ArcGIS 10.1 (Esri, Redlands, CA).
evidence: The claim describes the methodology for obtaining HbS data with citation.

claim: Predicted allele frequencies for G6PDd were extracted for each PSU waypoint from continuous global predicted surface maps.
source: Predicted allele frequencies for HbS (Piel et al., 2013) and G6PDd (Howes et al., 2012) were extracted for each PSU waypoint from continuous global predicted surface maps of the worldwide distribution of these genes using ArcGIS 10.1 (Esri, Redlands, CA).
evidence: The claim describes the methodology for obtaining G6PDd data with citation.

claim: The surface maps for HbS and G6PDd were generated as part of the Malaria Atlas Project (MAP), using Bayesian geostatistical models of prevalence data.
source: These surface maps were generated as part of the Malaria Atlas Project (MAP) (Malaria Atlas Project, 2013), using Bayesian geostatistical models of prevalence data collected from a systematic review of community-based surveys (Gething et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim describes the source and methodology for the genetic maps with citations.

claim: Information regarding children's vaccination and vitamin A supplementation history was ascertained from health card data recorded during the survey interview.
source: Information regarding children's vaccination and vitamin A supplementation history was ascertained from health card data recorded during the survey interview.
evidence: The claim describes the data collection method for vaccination history.

claim: Children whose mother/guardian responded in the affirmative to vaccination but did not provide health cards to document this information were excluded from the analysis.
source: Children whose mother/guardian responded in the affirmative to vaccination (e.g. child vaccinated during campaign) but did not provide health cards to document this information were excluded from the analysis.
evidence: The claim describes an exclusion criterion for the analysis.

claim: The microscopic presence of Plasmodium spp. was determined by reading Giemsa-stained thick blood films.
source: The microscopic presence of Plasmodium spp. was determined by reading Giemsa-stained thick blood films.
evidence: The claim describes the laboratory methodology for parasitemia detection.

claim: Capillary blood was collected during household interviews and tested onsite for malaria antigenemia.
source: Capillary blood was collected during household interviews and tested onsite for malaria antigenemia.
evidence: The claim describes the blood collection and testing procedure.

claim: Pƒ-specific HRP-2 antigens were detected using the rapid diagnostic Paracheck Pf for Burkina Faso and Senegal surveys.
source: Pƒ-specific HRP-2 antigens were detected using the rapid diagnostic Paracheck Pf (Orchid Biomedical Services, Goa, India) for Burkina Faso and Senegal surveys and first response malaria antigen HRP-2 (Premier Medical Corporation, Daman, India) for the Rwanda survey.
evidence: The claim describes the diagnostic test used in specific countries.

claim: Pƒ-specific HRP-2 antigens were detected using first response malaria antigen HRP-2 for the Rwanda survey.
source: Pƒ-specific HRP-2 antigens were detected using the rapid diagnostic Paracheck Pf (Orchid Biomedical Services, Goa, India) for Burkina Faso and Senegal surveys and first response malaria antigen HRP-2 (Premier Medical Corporation, Daman, India) for the Rwanda survey.
evidence: The claim describes the diagnostic test used in Rwanda.

claim: Thick blood smears were prepared by trained technicians for all children and sent for gold standard testing of malaria to designated laboratories in each country.
source: Thick blood smears were prepared by trained technicians for all children, and sent for gold standard testing of malaria to the Centre National de Recherche et de Formation sur le Paludisme (Burkina Faso), Centro de Investigações em Saúde de Manhiça (Mozambique), TRAC/Plus Malaria Unit in Kigali (Rwanda) and Department of Parasitology at the Université Cheikh Anta Diop (Senegal).
evidence: The claim describes the laboratory testing procedures.

claim: Internal quality control was conducted using standard laboratory protocol and procedures, including having slides randomly read by different laboratory technicians or the chief technician/supervisor.
source: Internal quality control was conducted using standard laboratory protocol and procedures, including having slides randomly read by different laboratory technicians or the chief technician/supervisor for internal quality control measures.
evidence: The claim describes the quality control procedures.

claim: External quality control for Mozambique included selecting samples by a computerized system developed by ICF Macro and sending them for external quality control testing at the Muraz Center.
source: External quality control (Mozambique only) included selecting samples by a computerized system developed by ICF Macro and sending them for external quality control testing at the Muraz Center (Bobo-Dioulasso).
evidence: The claim describes the external quality control procedures for Mozambique.

claim: Capillary blood was collected during household interviews from all women aged 15–29 years for HIV testing.
source: Capillary blood was collected during household interviews from all women aged 15–29 years.
evidence: The claim describes the HIV testing sample collection.

claim: Samples for HIV testing were collected on filter paper, dried for 24 hr and then sent for testing to designated laboratories in each country.
source: Samples were collected on filter paper, dried for 24 hr and then sent for testing to the Centre Regional de Transfusion Sanguine de Ouagadougou (Burkina Faso), National Reference Laboratory (Rwanda) and National Reference Laboratory of Bacteriology and Virology at A Le Dantec Hospital (Senegal).
evidence: The claim describes the HIV sample processing and testing procedures.

claim: Viral antibodies for HIV were detected using the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)-based assay VironostikaÒ HIV Uni-Form II plus O.
source: Viral antibodies were detected using the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)-based assay VironostikaÒ HIV Uni-Form II plus O (Biomériux, Marcy l'Etoile, France).
evidence: The claim describes the HIV testing methodology.

claim: Positive HIV samples and a portion of negative samples were tested using the ELISA assay EnzygnostÒ Anti-HIV ½ plus.
source: Positive samples and a portion of negative samples were tested using the ELISA assay EnzygnostÒ Anti-HIV ½ plus (Siemens AG, Erlangen, Germany).
evidence: The claim describes the confirmatory HIV testing methodology.

claim: Discordant HIV samples were further tested using the Pepti Lav assay or InnoLia.
source: Discordant samples were further tested using the Pepti Lav assay (Bio-Rad Laboratories, Hercules, CA) or InnoLia (Burkina Faso and Rwanda).
evidence: The claim describes the tie-breaker HIV testing methodology.

claim: Multivariable logistic regression models were used to estimate associations between malaria and childhood vaccination/supplementation.
source: Multivariable logistic regression models were used to estimate associations between malaria and childhood vaccination/supplementation.
evidence: The claim describes the statistical analysis methodology.

claim: Country and PSU were defined as strata, and households as clusters using logistic regression models that accounted for the complex survey data structure.
source: To avoid statistical inference errors in our results due to clustering and stratification from the sampling process, we defined country and PSU as strata, and households as clusters using logistic regression models that accounted for the complex survey data structure.
evidence: The claim describes the statistical methodology for handling complex survey data.

claim: Propensity scores were used to control for differences in patient characteristics associated with vaccine or vitamin use by inverse probability weighting of models.
source: Due to the observational nature of the data (not randomized), we controlled for differences in patient characteristics associated with vaccine or vitamin use, by inverse probability weighting of models using the propensity score for receiving a vaccine or vitamin supplement.
evidence: The claim describes the methodology for addressing selection bias.

claim: Standardized bias measures were used to assess numerical balance in propensity score covariate distributions, before and after IPW weighting.
source: Standardized bias measures were used to assess numerical balance in propensity score covariate distributions, before and after IPW weighting (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim describes the methodology for assessing balance in propensity score models.

claim: Factors with standardized bias values ≤0.25 were considered balanced.
source: Factors with standardized bias values ≤0.25 were considered balanced.
evidence: The claim describes the criterion for assessing balance.

claim: Prior to enrolling in the survey, the parent/adult responsible for the child had to provide written informed consent to participate, along with additional informed consent for blood sample collection and testing.
source: Prior to enrolling in the survey, the parent/adult responsible for the child had to provide written informed consent to participate, along with additional informed consent for blood sample collection and testing.
evidence: The claim describes the ethical procedures for consent.

claim: If a child tested positive during the survey using malaria RDT, their parent/guardian was informed of results and the child was immediately given treatment according to the current treatment guidelines.
source: If a child tested positive during the survey using malaria RDT, their parent/guardian was informed of results and the child was immediately given treatment according to the current treatment guidelines.
evidence: The claim describes the ethical procedures for managing positive malaria results.

claim: HIV tests for adults were anonymous, with survey data only being linked to test results after respondent identifiers were deleted from the database.
source: HIV tests for adults were anonymous, with survey data only being linked to test results after respondent identifiers were deleted from the database.
evidence: The claim describes the ethical procedures for HIV testing confidentiality.

claim: HIV test results were not available to study participants, but patients were offered cards enabling them to obtain free HIV testing and counselling at Voluntary Testing Centers.
source: Although HIV test results were not available to study participants, patients were offered cards enabling them to obtain free HIV testing and counselling at Voluntary Testing Centers.
evidence: The claim describes the ethical procedures for HIV testing and counseling access.

claim: The Institutional Review Board of ICF Macro reviewed and approved the MEASURE Demographic and Health Surveys Project Phase III, in compliance with U.S. DHHS regulation 45 CFR 46 for 'Protection of Human Subjects' research.
source: The Institutional Review Board of ICF Macro reviewed and approved the MEASURE Demographic and Health Surveys Project Phase III, in compliance with United States (U.S.) Department of Health and Human Services (DHHS) regulation 45 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) 46 for 'Protection of Human Subjects' research.
evidence: The claim describes the ethical approval for the DHS surveys.

claim: Geographical waypoints were randomly displaced to ensure confidentiality (Urban PSU: positional error of 0–2 km; and, Rural PSU: positional error of 0–5 km (99% of clusters), or 0–10 km error (1% of clusters)).
source: Geographical waypoints were randomly displaced to ensure confidentiality [Urban PSU: positional error of 0–2 km; and, Rural PSU: positional error of 0–5 km (99% of clusters), or 0–10 km error (1% of clusters)].
evidence: The claim describes the confidentiality procedures for geographical data.

claim: As a secondary analysis of publically available de-identified data, the study was determined exempt from ethics review by Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health IRB Office according to U.S. DHHS regulation 45 CFR 46.102 for non-human subject research.
source: As a secondary analysis of publically available de-identified data, the study was determined exempt from ethics review by Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health IRB Office according to U.S. DHHS regulation 45 CFR 46.102 for non-human subject research.
evidence: The claim describes the ethical status of the secondary analysis.
